title: Assault on Precinct 13
full_review:
John Carpenter's 1976 film -- a cult classic -- is back with a twist. In this updated adaptation, the bad guys are cops.
"Assault on Precinct 13" (Rogue) is a brutal and violent -- though reasonably gripping -- story of a desolate Detroit police precinct under siege by crooked police who are out to silence a criminal (Laurence Fishburne) incarcerated there, to cover up what he knows about corruption within their ranks, effecting an unusual alliance between the police and criminals within the precinct who must unite to defend themselves.
The film opens on a horrific sequence showing an undercover drug bust going awry. Sgt. Jake Roenick (Ethan Hawke) is wracked by guilt when his colleagues are killed after he instructs them to run in the wrong direction.

Flash ahead: Roenick is now under the care of a police psychiatrist, Alex Sabian (Maria Bello), who pays him visits at the station house to get to the root of a psychological scarring which has left him largely dysfunctional. Banter between them indicates that there's a mutual attraction despite her protestations to the contrary.

It's a snowy New Year's Eve, and the staff of Precinct 13 is getting ready to celebrate the holiday. That includes Officer Jasper O'Shea (Brian Dennehy), sexy secretary Iris Ferry (Drea de Matteo), and Lt. Holloway (Peter Bryant).

A bus transferring prisoners to another facility for the night is ordered to drop off its load at Precinct 13, because of the hazardous driving conditions, and though Roenick is unhappy to accept his new charges, he reluctantly takes in Beck (John Leguizamo), Smiley (hip-hop performer Jeffrey "Ja Rule" Atkins), Anna (Aisha Hinds), and Marion Bishop (Fishburne), a dangerous crime kingpin and cop killer. (In an earlier scene, Bishop remarks that he has no faith, since he observed many convicts on death row imploring God's help with no discernible result.)

Bishop has been in nefarious cahoots with some top-level corrupt cops, headed by Marcus Duvall (Gabriel Byrne), head of the organized crime and racketeering squad, and it is they (in masked disguise) who now surround the precinct, hoping to kill Bishop before he spills the beans about his police connection and fingers them in court.

Roenick refuses to surrender Bishop, so the bad cops go all-out to kill everyone within the station house. They've cut the phone lines, jammed the cell phone frequencies, and because the building is in a remote area, the trapped occupants, who of course include Roenick's pretty shrink, have no recourse but to fight their way out.

As the siege intensifies, Roenick unlocks the prisoners and arms them to ward off their assailants outside.

That's the setup for an increasingly tense standoff with the bad guys gradually making inroads on the friends-in-adversity team inside. And there's the underlying tension of never knowing whether the criminals inside the station house will turn on their newfound allies.

Fishburne is a powerful presence -- even when he's not speaking -- and Hawke gives a textured performance as the cop with a tortured past, who overcomes his lethargy under extraordinary circumstances. Strange bedfellows though these characters are, the actors make you believe an alliance is possible. Leguizamo is especially good as the wound-up junkie and Dennehy as a hothead cop. Robert Gantz's gritty photography enhances the doom-laden atmosphere.

Jean-Francois Richet's remake of the 1976 film has its share of suspenseful moments, but the bloodshed and violence seem unnecessarily explicit, and the improbable story calls for major suspension of disbelief, at times provoking unwanted audience titters.

Carpenter's original film, which had its roots in Howard Hawks' "Rio Bravo," has been adapted by James DeMonaco into what the filmmakers call an "urban Western." The migraine-inducing soundtrack, with its explosions and gunfire, culminates in an equally ear-assaulting rap song over the credits.

Again, this film is loaded with violence, but for an action film the attention to characterization and good performances make this several cuts above the usual mindless mayhem movie.

The film has graphic and bloody violence and related gore, much rough, crude and profane language and some sexual innuendo. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is L -- limited adult audience, films whose problematic content many adults would find troubling. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted.
